title: Rookies and Second-Year Players: How to Value Them
brief: How much should we pay for rookies and second-year players, and how long should we hold them in season before cutting? It must cover the year-two jump, year-three breakout odds by price, rookie point guard struggles, the Thanksgiving rule and why Summer League numbers mislead.
summary: Pay real money only for second-year players with a top-100 price tag. Treat rookies as cheap end-of-draft flyers and nominate at most one or two of them. A rookie with a real role gets until Thanksgiving (2026-11-26) to fix his efficiency. A rookie who is not playing gets two weeks.

sections.heading: Rookies at the auction: cheap flyers only

paragraphs.text: Do not overpay for rookies. At best, a draft class gives one top 50 player and three top 100 players. Most classes give only three or four relevant players at all. Drafters take far too many rookies near the end of drafts, so that is where they are most overrated.

In our league, 144 players are drafted. An uncertain rookie belongs in the flyer zone, around picks 120 to 130 in a 12-team league. That is the end of the active roster or the first bench slot. In our auction, that means the cheap bids late in the draft. Do not let a bidding war push a rookie up to what a reliable top-100 player costs. Rookies are usually drafted around pick 100, and early in the season they play like it.

Draft slot is not a reason to pay more. Being a top five NBA pick does not make a player great. Even strong classes have two or three top-10 picks who bust badly. Judge a rookie by his situation, minutes, usage and non-scoring stats. Rebounds and defensive stats give a rookie a baseline that can offset bad efficiency. That makes bigs with blocks and boards safer cheap flyers than guards who mostly score.

Ignore the 'most NBA ready' story for older rookies. They are usually older because they are not as good as the younger prospects. Players who are around 24 as rookies have rarely become NBA success stories. Rookies on deep teams may play about 28 minutes a night instead of 34 early on, so do not expect big scoring nights right away.

sections.heading: Rookie point guards and high-usage rookies

paragraphs.text: Rookie point guards are almost always bad for fantasy. Expect efficiency problems and be skeptical of them in redraft. The struggles are worst in the first two to three months. Some good players, such as De'Aaron Fox and Darius Garland, were never worth rostering as rookies.

This hits our categories directly. Rookie guards usually struggle with both efficiency and turnovers early. High-usage rookies nearly always post bad percentages. FG% and FT% are team ratios, so a high-volume rookie shooter drags them down the most. Turnovers count against us too. Guards with weak athleticism or strength look worst, especially when they are pushed into a defense-first role with little offensive work.
Rule for our draft: do not spend more than a flyer price on a rookie point guard. If you take one anyway, make sure the rest of your roster can absorb weak FG% and extra turnovers until December.

sections.heading: The year-two jump: where to spend

paragraphs.text: Second-year players are much more relevant than rookies. Over six years, top 50 category players went from 3 as rookies to 8 in year two. Top 100 players went from 11 to 31, and top 150 players went from 20 to 54. Across all rookies, 60% improved in year two, and 41% improved by at least 50 ranking slots. In recent years, the big breakouts have moved more to year two.

The jump mostly comes from players who already showed something. Rookie rank and sophomore rank have a correlation of about 0.61. Only 30 players in six years jumped from outside the top 150 to inside it. Young players usually gain usage and minutes each year, from a small rookie role to a bigger one by year three.

Market price is a good guide at the top end. All seven sophomores with a top 50 ADP finished top 100. Of those with an ADP of 51 to 100, 72% finished top 100. Second-year players priced as top-100 picks are sound buys at full value. Sophomores with an ADP of 101 to 150 hit only 13% of the time for top 100 and 33% for top 150. That range is the back third of our 144-player draft, so they are flyers, not sleepers. Undrafted sophomores almost never become relevant.

sections.heading: Year three and beyond: breakout odds by price

paragraphs.text: Year-three breakouts tend to come from players who did not take a step in year two. Third-year players drafted inside the top 50 have not busted badly. Those drafted between 101 and 150 made the top 100 only 13% of the time. Third-year players with no ADP almost never become top 100 players. Big jumps in year four are unlikely for players who showed nothing in their first three years.

For our last few auction slots, look at opportunity and situation first. With equal opportunity, lean toward a second-year player over a third-year player. Do not spend a bench slot on a fourth-year player whose only case is that a jump is 'due'. Rules like the third-year breakout are a baseline. Judge each player on his own situation after that.

The experts disagree on when young players matter. One view says rookies and second-year players usually do not help NBA teams win, and the leap tends to come in year three. Teams trying to win often bench their young players. The other view says the rookie wall and the sophomore slump are lazy myths. In that view, about 90% of rookies improve during the season, and the biggest breakouts now come in year two. In practice, trust the year-two data at auction. Check whether the team is a contender before you count on a young player's minutes.

Treat Summer League with heavy skepticism. Rookies play next to fringe players, and opposing defenses go all out to disrupt them. Summer League is for trial and error, so one bad shooting night, like 1-for-11 from three, should not count for much.

Shooting percentages are the most misleading part. Hot Summer League percentages are not sustainable, and Summer League three-point percentages should not be trusted. The stats that do carry over for rookies are assists, rebounds, blocks, three-point attempt rate and scoring. Steals have little correlation. Three-point attempt volume is the most useful single stat, because a willingness to shoot is a better signal than the make rate.

The notes differ slightly on percentages. One note says Summer League percentages have some correlation for rookies but none for second-year players. Others say shooting percentages carry over very little. Either way, do not raise a bid because of a hot shooting summer. Check whether the skills that made the player good showed up. Second-year players should dominate Summer League, so ordinary numbers from them are a disappointment, not a neutral result.
Preseason role news is more useful. If a rookie flyer is named a starter, move him up your list and be willing to pay a bit more for him.

sections.heading: In season: the Thanksgiving rule and when to cut

paragraphs.text: Top rookies often start slow, with poor efficiency for the first two months, and then improve in the second half. Rookies, especially guards, usually shoot badly for two to three months. If you drafted a rookie early, accept the slow start and do not drop him.

Use two clocks. If a rookie starts with real usage, or his role is fine or growing, hold him until about Thanksgiving (2026-11-26) before giving up, even if he hurts your efficiency. That also applies to a starting rookie point guard. If he is not playing at all, cut him after two weeks. You can pick him up again later if his role changes.

Do not hold several inefficient rookie flyers at once while you wait. Choose which ones to keep and drop the rest quickly. We have only 2 bench slots and 6 adds a week, so a second slow rookie costs you a streaming spot.

Keep watching the waiver wire late in the season. More rookies become relevant in the second half and in the fantasy playoffs, because of tanking, injuries and improvement. Our playoffs run in weeks 19 to 21 and end 2027-03-28. With less tanking expected this season, that late jump may be smaller than usual. Projections also assume trade candidates stay all season, so they can understate rookies stuck behind them. After the 2027-03-04 trade deadline, check which rookies gained minutes and bid FAB on them.
